purpose: Trihexyphenidyl is used to help control the muscle stiffness, tremors, and movement problems caused by Parkinson's disease. It is also used to treat similar movement side effects that can happen when you take certain psychiatric medications. It helps make moving around easier and more comfortable.
how_it_works: Your brain uses a chemical messenger called acetylcholine to send signals that control muscle movement. In Parkinson's disease, this chemical becomes out of balance and causes unwanted muscle stiffness and shaking. Trihexyphenidyl blocks some of those acetylcholine signals, which helps relax the muscles and reduce tremors.
common_side_effects: Dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, difficulty urinating, dizziness, drowsiness, upset stomach, and feeling nervous or confused. These effects are very common with this type of medication. Drinking water and sucking on sugar-free candy can help with dry mouth.
warnings: Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first — stopping too quickly can cause problems. Tell your doctor if you have glaucoma, an enlarged prostate, or heart problems, as this drug may not be safe for you. It can cause confusion, especially in older adults, so use extra caution. Avoid alcohol and be careful driving or operating machinery since it can cause drowsiness or blurred vision. Stay hydrated, especially in hot weather, as this medicine can reduce your ability to sweat.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose is 1 mg taken by mouth once a day. Your doctor will slowly increase the dose over time, usually to somewhere between 6 mg and 10 mg per day, split into 3 or 4 doses taken with meals. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose.
